item.title: Events related to Markus Reineke as Springer Chair
item.description:
This academic year, the Springer Chair (a visiting professorship at Utrecht University) has been given to Markus Reineke. He will be visiting us in February, and in this context we are organizing several events:

  • a colloquium talk on Tuesday, February 3, from 16 to 17, in Minaert 201
  • a lecture series on February 4, 9, and 10 (see the webpage for more details)
  • a problem session on Wednesday, February 11, from 13h15 to 15h00, in HFG 611
  • a 2-day workshop on February 23 and 24 (see the webpage for more details, note that capacity is very limited)

Everyone is cordially invited to the colloquium, lecture series, and problem session!

item.title: Workshop announcement: VBAC 2025 Quivers – Sheaves
item.description:
Together with Vicky Hoskins and Martijn Kool we are organizing the 2025 edition of VBAC: a conference series with a long-standing tradition. It is a 2-day workshop in Utrecht, May 14 and 15.

There is a website with all information, including the registration form. In the VBAC tradition, we have slots for contributed talks, by younger participants. There is some funding for younger participants too.

I hope to see many of you there!

item.title: Noncommutative algebraic geometry summer school in Antwerp
item.description:
This summer we are organizing a summer school in Antwerp, on noncommutative algebraic geometry (more precisely: homological mirror symmetry, and the formalism of $\mathrm{A}_\infty$-categories). It is organized with the help of SLMath, as an offshoot of last year's research semester on noncommutative algebraic geometry. The application form for non-US citizens is now available, and all information can be found on the workshop's website.

Please share this with interested students. The target audience is master students and early PhD students with some background in the topic.

item.title: Workshop announcement: GROW@Frankfurt
item.description:
Following a great tradition of US-based Graduate Research Opportunities for Women workshops, we organized a similar event in Bonn back in 2022, with editions in 2023 and 2024 that I seemingly did not advertise using blogposts. There is somewhat of a franchise behind it now.

I am now no longer an organizer on the European side, but I am happy to spread the word that the 2025 edition is taking place in Frankfurt.

item.title: Modern Methods in Moduli: a workshop in Luxembourg
item.description:
I am excited to announce that together with Sarah Scherotzke and Nicolò Sibilla we are organizing a 3-day workshop at the University of Luxembourg, titled Modern Methods in Moduli. It takes place from Tuesday November 26 to Thursday November 28, at the Belval campus. We already have a great lineup, and some more names will still be added to it.

We ask that everyone who plans on attending registers, so that we can arrange the coffee breaks accordingly. We have some funding for junior participants, you can indicate that you need funding on the registration form.

item.title: Upper-Rhine and Tributaries Algebraic Geometry Seminar
item.description:
I am really happy to announce URTAGS: the Upper-Rhine and Tributaries Algebraic Geometry Seminar, a joint seminar with the universities of of Basel, Freiburg, Lorraine, Luxembourg, Saarbrücken, Strasbourg, Stuttgart, and Tübingen.

The first edition is scheduled for June 25, and 2 or 3 editions per year (twice in the centrally located Strasbourg, once on location) are planned.

I hope to see some of you there!

item.title: Stacks Project Workshop 2023
item.description:
Great news! There will be another Stacks Project Workshop in 2023, again in Ann Arbor like the 2017 edition.

All information can be found on the website, including the registration, which is open until February 15, 2023.

item.title: Videos and notes of Noncommutative Shapes
item.description:
Last week we had Noncommutative Shapes, the birthday conference for Michel Van den Bergh. People seemed to have enjoyed the event a lot, so that makes me really happy as an organiser.

I've now posted the recordings to the Noncommutative Shapes YouTube channel, and the notes (whenever available) are also available from the conference website. So even if you had to miss the event, you can still enjoy the great talks that happened last week, I'm really grateful to the speakers for doing such a wonderful job.

item.title: Noncommutative Shapes
item.description: Postponed by 2 years because of the pandemic, but now it's finally there: Noncommutative Shapes, a birthday conference for Michel Van den Bergh. I am really stoked for this event, and I hope to see many familiar (and new) faces!

item.title: Workshop announcement: GROW@Bonn
item.description:
Today is the International Day of Women & Girls in Science, and this is a good opportunity to advertise an event we are organising at the University of Bonn:

GROW@Bonn

stands for Graduate Research Opportunities for Women (and the @Bonn only signifies that the event is taking place there, not that we claim it is the only place where this is possible, or where there seems to be room for improvement). It is modeled after earlier events in the United States (see e.g. the website for the 2021 edition).

item.title: Noncommutative Shapes: a half-way event
item.description:
Michel Van den Bergh turned 60 last year, and as with all birthday conferences they had to be postponed. Because organising a large in-person event still seems very hard, the big conference is meant to take place September 2022, but on Monday next week we will have a halfway-event, with three online speakers:

  • Yuri Manin, Quantisation in monoidal categories and quantum operads
  • Alexander Kuznetsov, Simultaneous categorical resolutions
  • Marco Gualtieri, From geometric quantization to noncommutative algebraic geometry

I'm very glad that we can have this small celebration in honour of Michel and his great work in (noncommutative) algebraic geometry!

item.title: Recordings and slides for the Felix Klein lectures by Markus Reineke
item.description:
The Felix Klein Lectures are over (they were great!), and all recordings and slides are available on the website.

I want to thank Markus again, for giving such a great lecture series, which involved improvising through power and internet outages, and quarantine. Thanks also to Paul Wedrich for dealing with the on-site aspect of the lecture series (and hence improvising through power and internet outages).

item.title: Registration for Felix Klein lectures by Markus Reineke
item.description:
The registration for the Felix Klein lectures by Markus Reineke is now open. Markus is a great lecturer, and he will talk about very exciting topics, so I strongly suggest anyone who might be interested in representation theory or algebraic geometry to register!

For good measure, here's the abstract again:

Quiver moduli spaces are algebraic varieties encoding the continuous parameters of linear algebra type classification problems. In recent years their topological and geometric properties have been explored, and applications to, among others, Donaldson-Thomas and Gromov-Witten theory have emerged.

item.title: Felix Klein lectures by Markus Reineke
item.description:
I'm happy to announce the (virtual) Felix Klein lectures by Markus Reineke, from the University of Bochum. They are virtually in Bonn, part of the junior trimester program on representation theory which I'm part of.

Markus will talk about Quiver moduli and applications, here's his abstract:

Quiver moduli spaces are algebraic varieties encoding the continuous parameters of linear algebra type classification problems. In recent years their topological and geometric properties have been explored, and applications to, among others, Donaldson-Thomas and Gromov-Witten theory have emerged.

item.title: Some updates
item.description:
Here are some small updates, which do not deserve a blogpost of their own as such.

  • Hodge diamond cutter now also computes Hodge diamonds for Fano varieties of linear subspaces on the intersection of 2 quadrics. For more on this, see (the references in) this MathOverflow post where I learned that these are objects that one can study.

  • I have updated the conference schedule at ncag.info because of COVID-19 cancellations and postponements. Please let me know if I've missed something, or if your conference is not listed there.

item.title: Seminar announcement: exceptional collections on partial flag varieties
item.description:
Next semester (which in Bonn runs from roughly April to July) we will be running a (graduate) seminar on exceptional collections, with a view towards partial flag varieties. The two main goals are:

  • to familiarise ourselves with derived categories of finite-dimensional algebras, and important concepts such as Ringel duality and quasi-hereditary algebras
  • to familiarise ourselves with the geometry of partial flag varieties, and their derived categories, to understand the existence and structure of exceptional collections

We will have an organisational meeting this Wednesday, at 10h15 in room 0.011. If you would like to give a talk but can't make it on Wednesday, please send me an email, especially if you are a Bonn graduate student.

item.description:

In fact, I have a 50% FWO appointment at the University of Antwerp starting October 1. This footnote serves as the public announcement of that I guess.

item.title: Live blogging the Antwerp conference (3)
item.description:
It sure was an exciting week! Also, the conference picture is available (thanks to Dennis Presotto's camera, and Mieke De Mulder's photography skills). Do not let the picture trick you into thinking that I am as tall as Michael Wemyss, I had the advantage of standing one step higher, and still I'm smaller.

Very soon there should be notes made by the participants on the website.

Friday September 23

The topic of Dimitri Kaledin's talk was somewhat related to questions I thought about in the beginning of my PhD, but I never got really far. He constructed a formalism for tackling gluing questions for enhanced triangulated categories, avoiding the framework of stable $\infty$-categories (because these are depending on who you ask either trivial, or impossible to work with) and pure dg categories (which is not the most flexible formalism). item.title: Live blogging the Antwerp conference (2)
item.description:
Wednesday September 21

Bertrand Toën talked about his approach to a proof of Bloch's conjecture, mentioned before on my blog. Back then it was exciting stuff, and after his overview talk it still is very cool to see how it is possible to apply noncommutative algebraic geometry to problems of an arithmetic nature.

He mentioned that a strong version of resolution of singularities would also settle the conjecture, because of a special case of the conjecture proven by Kato–Saito that would imply the whole thing provided this mythical result. Using noncommutative algebro-geometric techniques seems like a more fun thing to do from my perspective.

item.title: Live blogging the Antwerp conference
item.description:
Reading my blog you could've figured out that we are having a big conference in Antwerp. Yesterday was too hectic to liveblog this, as the neverending author noticed, so I guess I'll just do one post every two days.

Monday September 19

Ragnar Buchweitz quoted the following joke that Matt Satriano (he heard it from Dick Gross) made last week in Banff:

A good talk should contain one joke and one proof, and you should be able to tell them apart.

I think Ragnar turned the punchline into and they should not be the same, which works equally well. Taking this advice from Ragnar (or Matt, or Dick) I might focus my discussion a little bit on the jokes the speakers made, rather than give a detailed outline of what they talked about.

item.title: Announcing a seminar
item.description:
To make sense of the next post, and potentially attract more attendees, I want to announce a student seminar on algebra and algebraic geometry at the University of Antwerp. It's called ANAGRAMS, which is an acronym for "Antwerp algebraic geometry, rings and more seminar".

All the interesting information can be found on the website, to summarise: PhD students give lectures for PhD students on subjects related to algebraic geometry and algebra (based on the research areas we are active in). We pick a subject, work on it for a few weeks, then take another one. It's about learning things, it's not a research seminar.
